question: In France, all collective management organisations (CMOs) representing performers and authors in the music sector have made use of the provisions contained in Article 4 of the Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market1 and have ‘opted-out’ with respect to the works and performances they represent (i.e. their ‘repertoire’). Suno and Udio are two US-based providers of AI generated music.

They are currently in litigation with Warner Music and Sony Music, two major record labels, and have already settled with Universal Music. Being online products, Suno and Udio are also available in the European digital single market.

As such, they should be obliged to respect the current European laws on copyright and related rights, including Article 4(3) of the Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market and specifically the ‘opt-out’ exercised by the aforementioned French CMOs.

Can the Commission confirm that, if companies offering a product similar to that of Suno and Udio wish to offer their services in the EU, they must in all cases respect and comply with the opt-out expressed by the French CMOs and specifically in all cases they must obtain explicit authorisation from said CMOs prior to using their repertoire?
OJ L 130, 17.5.2019, pp. 92–125, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/790/oj.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.2.

2026) Assuming that the referred French collective management organisations have appropriately exercised the rights reservation in accordance with the criteria established in Article 4(3) of the Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market (DSM)1 as implemented in French law, third parties may no longer reproduce in France the concerned works and other subject matter under the text and data mining (TDM) exception.
TDM processing would henceforth require prior authorisation from the concerned rightsholders, including when it is used for the training of AI models.

The AI Act2 requires providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models that place their model on the EU market to put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law and in particular to identify and comply with a reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) DSM Directive.

This obligation applies regardless of the jurisdiction in which the copyrightrelevant acts underpinning the training of those GPAI models take place3. To the extent that providers of GPAI models placing their model on the EU market have carried out TDM on copyright-protected content to train their models, they must respect a reservation of rights made by the relevant rightholders.
The Copyright Chapter of the Code of Practice on GeneralPurpose AI4 sets out how providers of GPAI models that are signatories to that Code intend to comply with that obligation.

In this regard, the Commission launched a process to facilitate the identification of and general agreement on opt-out protocols that can be considered as state-of-the-art, technically implementable, and widely adopted by rightsholders across different cultural and creative sectors (as specified in Measure 1.3. of the Copyright Section of the Code).
1 Directive (EU) 2019/790 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on copyright and
related rights in the Digital Single Market and amending Directives 96/9/EC and 2001/29/EC. https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/790/oj.

2 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act). https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng.
